parts:
Dear INLA team,

i'm currently investigating how to use INLA approach to fit a DLM with a trigonometric 2-harmonics seasonal component.

So far i've been using the 'dlm' package, but i'm assessing how to switch to INLA approach for later more flexibility (e.g. apply a censored model).

In a first step, i'm trying to fit a DLM with INLA with the similar model as i've been using with 'dlm', that is: a 2 order polynomial component + a trigonometry 2-harmonics seasonal component (supposing that 2 cycles are likely to occur by year)

I've investigated the DLM examples provided at http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/papers/DLM_examples_11112010.R (together with the report)


I attach here the code that i've put in place (with some fake timeserie to reproduce the example).
So far, i think what i have a only set-up a single harmonic for the seasonal component... i'm quite stuck about how to add a second harmonic, as the way to code is slightly different from the 'dlm' package.

Could somebody give me advice:
(1) if they are issues in this example code, and hopefully (2) how i could set-up a second harmonic in the seasonal component..

I thank you very much in advance for your help

Best regards,
Emmanuel

parts:
In accord to the specification in page 44, the observation equation
depends on two terms T_t and H_t. H_t is a first order harmonic and T_t
is a second order random walk. Do you want second order in the harmonic
term too?

On 15/01/15 10:40, emmanuel...@gmail.com wrote:
> Mumps example seems a first order model, and the seasonality seems to be modeled with a single harmonic.

parts: Hi Emmanuel,

On 26/01/15 11:06, Emmanuel Blondel wrote:
What i'm trying to produce with inla is a a 2d order dlm that includes a seasonal component made of 2 harmonics. Adding 2 harmonics allows me to get peaks that i would not expect with a single harmonic.
I attach a new script (with test data, so you can reproduce it), where i've now specified these 2 harmonics. For this i've relied on the 2d order dlm example provided by Ruiz-Cardenas et al., and used the 'mumps' example as basis for specying trigonometric harmonic seasonal component.

I'm not sure which model you are trying to fit... From the index set for the data (1:n part) in your code I see thay you fit the following
   y_t = x_t + a1_t + b1_t + a2_t + b2_t
where, as I understood x_t is second order RW and the a1, a2, b1 and b2 terms have all 'rw1' prior.

For information, i also attach a plot where i've compared the result with the dlm package.
It's not clear to me what's the hidden part that would explain the difference between inla and dlm fitted models. Would you have any advice on this? or remark to improve the attached code?

I'm not sure what are you comparing... Following the DLM language in the above model, INLA does not return posterior marginals for y_i, only for x_i. To have a proper advice I have to know what exact are you plotting.

Elias.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: dlm with a trigonometric 2-harmonics seasonal component
parts:
Hi,

since you have Gaussian data, there shouldn't be much difference as all
calculations are exact, only some integral are approximated with
numerical integrals.

It can be a bit tricky to get everything in the model exactly the same,
which you need if you compare with dlm. Also dlm is a frequentisitic
analysis, right?

if you fix hyperparmaeters then you should be able to compare the two
approaches, I think.

you asked about suggestions to improve, and from computationall side, it
is tempting to try to reduce the number of hyperparmeters, like making
the precision for h1cos the same as for h1sin, and simular for h2cos and
h2sin (or all the same precision?)

H

> In order to compare both approaches, is there a way in INLA to fix
> the observation variance?

variance = 1.981

inla(....,
family = "gaussian",
control.family = list(hyper = list(prec = list(initial =
log(1/variance),fixed=TRUE)))
